newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern sells $4.3 billion in bonds.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern sells $4.3 billion in bonds.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. sold a record $4.3 billion in investment-grade bonds Wednesday to finance its acquisition of part of Conrail Inc.
In April, Norfolk Southern and CSX Corp. of Richmond, Va., agreed to a joint acquisition of Philadelphia-based Conrail for $10.3 billion.
Under the deal, Norfolk agreed to pay $5.9 billion for 58 percent of Conrail's assets. CSX agreed to pay $4.3 billion for the remaining 42 percent of the East Coast railroad.
The Norfolk Southern bond sale topped what had been the biggest investment-grade bond issue -- U.S. West Inc.'s $4.1 billion sale of bonds in January.

Norfolk Southern's offering consisted of eight different types of bonds with maturities ranging from three years to 100 years. The notes were sold at yields ranging from 6.75 percent on the 3-year bonds to 7.91 percent on the 100-year bonds.

The bonds were rated BAA1 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB-plus by Standard & Poor's, a notch or two above junk-bond status. While the bonds are less risky than high-yield, high-risk junk bonds, they are more susceptible to changes in business conditions than higher-rated issues.

"This transaction is a vote of confidence in the reputation of Norfolk Southern as a good operator of a railroad company and for our financial strength," said William Romig, the company's vice president and treasurer.
He said the company increased the offering to $4.3 billion from $3 billion as a result of strong investor demand for the bonds.
Analysts confirmed investors were optimistic about the outlook for the company.

"Basically, Norfolk Southern has been the best-run among the major railroads," said Gary Sparago, corporate bond aanlyst for Deutsch Morgan Grenfell. "They should be an even stronger competitor following integration of the Conrail properties."
Analysts said a rally in the Treasury bond market Wednesday, aided by a government report of lower wholesale inflation last month, also contributed to the success of the deal.

Despite the positive market reception, one week prior to the offering both Moody's and Standard & Poor's cut Norfolk Southern's credit rating, citing concerns about its increased debt load following the acquisition.
Romig said the company's goal is to restore its credit rating to the level prior to the merger by paying off the debt over time with cash generated from its operations.
On May 1, CSX sold over $2 billion in bonds to finance its part of the acquisition.
Merrill Lynch & Co. and J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. co-led the Norfolk Southern offering.
